title: Two commuting hacks
content:
Just about everyone commutes to work, by car or by public transit. And just about everyone carries a smart phone.

All organizations have a communications problem, and it gets worse as they grow. Which issues are we facing today? Who else is on the team? What’s changed in the environment, and what do we need to get in sync on?

Consider starting an internal podcast. Just fifteen or twenty minutes a day. The host interviews team members, informs on important issues or simply helps people see the big picture. When everyone on the team listens to the same podcast each morning, cohesion and focus improve.

A podcast with 25 of the right listeners might be exactly the right size.

The second hack: I’m amazed at how many people on the train are mindlessly swiping through one social media platform or another. Judging by their facial expressions, they’re not enjoying it much.

Instead, we can focus our time and energy on learning. Six months of commuting can easily cover an advanced college course in something that interests us. And using Claude as a Socratic tutor can be a breakthrough. If you’re driving, use voice mode. Ask it to patiently engage you, one conversation at a time, in a journey to learn something difficult. How transistors work. Why the Roman Empire fell. The origin of species.

Day by day, your commute gets better and you get smarter.

[DN](http://nautil.us/author/david-nield)

Dwarf reedsnakes of the genus _Pseudorabdion_, found in Southeast Asia, have a rather clever way of fleeing from trouble: They turn cartwheels until they’re safe from danger. See for yourself:

Now, researchers have finally figured out how they do it, studying the action on video from multiple angles. Very precise, coordinated body movements keep the head of the snake stable and facing the direction of travel, while the rest of its body rotates.

This gets around the main issue with rolling as a way of locomotion, as you’ll know if you’ve ever gone headfirst down a hill: It’s a real challenge to see where you’re going and keep traveling in the same direction. The faster the speed, the more difficult it gets, which isn’t ideal when you’re fleeing from predators.

[Subscribe to skip ads](http://nautil.us/products)Advertisement

But is it effective?

**Read more: “**[**This Snake’s Tail Has a Fake “Spider” at the Tip**](https://nautil.us/this-snakes-tail-has-a-fake-spider-at-the-tip-1284917)**”**

With this method, snakes can move approximately 8 mph—four times faster than they can get around using traditional wriggling, and significantly faster than the average human jogger.

Here are the particulars behind the movement: The part of the snake’s body in contact with the ground rolls and lifts the anterior portion of the snake, including the head, until the tip of its tail is the only part touching the floor. The tail then pushes off into a new loop, and the cycle continues.

The researchers detailed the specific rolling movements used by the snakes. _Credit: Kojima et al., Current Biology, 2026_

This isn’t the normal way of getting about for the dwarf reedsnake, but it does seem to come into play when they need to escape something in a hurry. In fact, the researchers say the snakes tended to dive underneath nearby objects for extra cover after rolling.

We wouldn’t recommend such cartwheels when making your own quick getaways, though. Unless, maybe, you’re Buffy the Vampire Slayer. ![Image 8](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Early Humans in America Endured Climate Chaos
content:
Some 23,000 years ago, during the coldest part of the last ice age, people walked across the muddy margins of an ancient lake in what is now White Sands national park, New Mexico.

The footprints they left behind have transformed our understanding of when people [first reached the Americas](https://theconversation.com/topics/early-humans-1659?page=3). When we [reported dates](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.abg7586) for the White Sands footprints in 2021, our findings were met with controversy. They placed people in North America thousands of years earlier than other widely accepted sites.

[Subsequent work](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adh5007) using several independent dating techniques strengthened that chronology. [Our latest research](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aeh0707) takes the story [a step further](https://www.mdpi.com/2813-6284/4/3/22). Rather than simply asking when people were at White Sands, we can begin to ask: what sort of world did they experience?

The answer is a surprisingly dynamic one that was marked by periods of rapid climate change. Our expanded excavations at White Sands have identified 20 different horizons or packages of sediment containing human footprints. Together they span almost two millennia, from about 23,500 to 21,700 years ago, firmly within the last glacial maximum (the height of the last ice age).

Alongside the footprints, the sediments contain a remarkable archive of environmental change. Pollen records the vegetation growing around the basin, while organic molecules preserved in the sediment – including waxes originally produced by plant leaves – provide information about temperature and rainfall.

Together, these allowed us to reconstruct the landscape through which people were walking.

At the beginning of the record, White Sands looked very different from today. A large body of water, Lake Otero, [occupied much of the basin](https://www.nps.gov/whsa/learn/geology-of-white-sands.htm). The surrounding mountains supported conifer forests and average annual temperatures were around 4°C colder than today.

But conditions did not remain stable. From around 23,600 years ago the lake began to shrink as temperatures rose. Conifer forest declined and was increasingly replaced by oak and sagebrush.

Reconstruction of life at White Sands at the height of the last ice age. Credit: _Davide Bonadonna / Bournemouth University_

As a result of this warming, the basin became progressively drier as evaporation increased. Superimposed upon this longer term change were much sharper climatic swings.

Around 23,200 years ago, for example, White Sands experienced a short but severe drought. Rainfall declined, the lake became more saline and drought-tolerant vegetation expanded. This dry period coincided with a rapid climatic change recorded thousands of miles away in Greenland ice cores.

And people were there. Indeed, the earliest footprint horizon in our expanded sequence occurs around this climatic transition. Footprints continue to occur at intervals as the lake retreated and the environment changed.

Our new evidence therefore shows that people visited this landscape repeatedly while experiencing substantial environmental change.

Map of early archaeological sites in North America. _Credit: Datawrapper_

**Rapidly Changing World**

The footprints capture a world changing on timescales that could have been noticed by the people living there at the time. It is tempting to go one step further.

Were people particularly attracted to White Sands during difficult climatic episodes? Did the shrinking lake concentrate animals, plants or other resources that made the basin especially important during drought?

Perhaps. But footprints come with an important catch. What gets preserved is not necessarily a full picture of what happened. In a separate recent study, we used an [agent-based computer model](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-90-481-8927-4) to explore what a footprint record such as White Sands actually represents. Agent-based models are rather different from conventional models that attempt to predict something such as tomorrow’s weather.

Radiocarbon dates on seeds found at the site were one way that scientists determine the age of the footprints. Here, archaeologists record the placement of seeds. _Credit: National Park Service_

Instead, they populate a simplified world with individual “agents” following basic rules. Complex patterns can then emerge from their collective behaviour. Our virtual world consisted of people moving around a fluctuating lake.

When they crossed mud they left footprints. Those footprints gradually disappeared unless changing water levels created the right conditions for them to be buried and preserved.

The result was revealing. People could be active around the lake while leaving virtually no fossil record. At other times, relatively few people could produce large numbers of preserved footprints. What mattered was not simply whether people were present, but whether their presence happened to coincide with the right geological circumstances.

**Arriving in Pulses**

Preservation was particularly likely during environmental transitions. A dry period could expose large areas of footprint forming mud. Subsequent wetting and sedimentation could then bury the tracks and preserve them. When we compared this model with the real White Sands record, we found something striking.

The footprint surfaces occur as irregular pulses that tend to cluster around periods of climatic and hydrological change – just the pattern predicted by the model.

Footprints are snapshots, not a movie. But this study changes how the White Sands record should be interpreted. The footprints demonstrate unequivocally that people were present at particular moments.

People repeatedly crossed this landscape for almost two millennia while the regional climate swung between wetter and exceptionally dry conditions. _Credit: National Park Service_

But the gaps between footprint surfaces do not demonstrate that people were absent. Nor does a surface covered in footprints necessarily indicate a population boom. A handful of people repeatedly crossing soft ground can leave hundreds of tracks.

So we should be cautious about turning the correlation between footprints and climate into a simple story in which people arrived at White Sands whenever drought struck. Instead, there are two histories intertwined here.

One is a human history: people repeatedly inhabited this landscape for almost two millennia while the lake shrank, vegetation changed and the regional climate swung between wetter and exceptionally dry conditions. The other is a geological history determining which tiny fragments of those human lives happened to survive.

Footprints provide an intimate connection with ancient people, but they are not a continuous record of their lives. They are individual frames – moments when human behaviour, mud, water and chance came together. ![Image 1](https://assets.nautil.us/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)![Image 2](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)![Image 3](https://assets.nautil.us/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: AI Proved the Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis. What Happens Now?
content:
Among the 377 results that OpenAI [announced](https://www.quantamagazine.org/updates/transformation/#167703) on October 6, 2026, one stood out. It claimed to settle the “quasi-Riemann hypothesis” — a weaker version of the Riemann hypothesis, which is arguably the biggest open question in math. The new proof is, as [Jared Duker Lichtman (opens a new tab)](https://mathematics.stanford.edu/people/jared-duker-lichtman) of Stanford University put it, “the most significant AI-for-math achievement so far, by quite a margin.”

The Riemann hypothesis has been an open problem for over 160 years. Resolving it would enable mathematicians to better understand the nature of prime numbers, one of math’s most crucial building blocks. And that’s just for starters.

The implications of even the more limited “quasi-RH” result are “staggering,” said [Maksym Radziwiłł (opens a new tab)](https://maksym-radziwill.github.io/) of New York University. “In a sense, the vast majority of consequences of RH already follow from quasi-RH.”

Moreover, contrary to what mathematicians had long expected, the proof didn’t need to introduce any new concepts — it instead unearthed hidden connections between old ones. “The proof is a surprising synthesis of well-known ideas,” said [Alexander Dunn (opens a new tab)](https://alexjdunn.weebly.com/) of the Georgia Institute of Technology.

The result relied in part on techniques pioneered by Radziwiłł and Dunn. Alongside other number theorists, they have been working to understand the proof and what it could mean. Now they’re starting to get answers.

## **To Zeta and Beyond**

To understand what the quasi-Riemann hypothesis says, you first have to understand the Riemann hypothesis. When the Clay Mathematics Institute [announced (opens a new tab)](https://www.claymath.org/millennium-problems/) seven Millennium Prize Problems at the turn of the century, the Riemann hypothesis loomed above the other six. It was the only one carried over from the [celebrated agenda-setting list (opens a new tab)](https://www.simonsfoundation.org/news/solved-unsolved-and-unsolvable-the-status-of-hilberts-23-problems-in-mathematics/) of problems that David Hilbert had announced a century earlier.

On its surface, the conjecture concerns the behavior of a particular function. Start with the sum 1+1 2+1 3+1 4+⋯. Now use that sum (together with a special mathematical trick to extend its scope) to build a more general function, called the Riemann zeta (ζ) function:

ζ(s)=1+1 2 s+1 3 s+1 4 s+⋯

Here, the input _s_ is a complex number. Complex numbers have two parts —a “real” part and an “imaginary” part, which is a multiple of the square root of −1 (written as _i_). Any complex number can be thought of as a point on a plane:

![Image 1](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RiemannsTheory-Fig1-crMarkBelan-Desktop-v2-1.svg)![Image 2](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RiemannsTheory-Fig1-crMarkBelan-Mobile-v2.svg)

Mark Belan/_Quanta Magazine_

The Riemann hypothesis is about which values of _s_ will make the zeta function equal zero.

But it is also about far more than how this particular function behaves. As Bernhard Riemann realized when he first made the conjecture in 1859, the function relates to patterns in the prime numbers —integers divisible only by 1 and themselves that many mathematicians call the “atoms of arithmetic.”

It’s long been known that as you move along the number line, the primes thin out. Riemann showed that exactly _how_ the primes thin out is, in a sense, governed by the zeta function — in particular by the places where it equals zero.

It’s straightforward to prove that if _s_ is a negative even number (−2, −4, −6, …), then ζ(_s_) = 0. These are called trivial zeros. The Riemann hypothesis says that the only other zeros of the zeta function, called nontrivial zeros, occur when _s_ has a real part of 1/2. That is, they should all be located on a vertical line:

![Image 3](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RiemannsTheory-Fig2-crMarkBelan-Desktop-v2-1.svg)![Image 4](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RiemannsTheory-Fig2-crMarkBelan-Mobile-v2.svg)

If any nontrivial zero were to be found somewhere away from that vertical line, it would imply that the primes must form an extremely surprising pattern, one that has never been observed to date.

Just narrowing the area where the nontrivial zeros can appear has had huge ramifications. Riemann himself proved that nontrivial zeros of the zeta function can only be found in a vertical strip between zero and 1. Then, in 1896, two mathematicians showed that zeros could not lie on the edges of the strip. As a direct consequence, they were able to prove an important result called the prime number theorem, a formula for how quickly, on average, the primes thin out.

If the Riemann hypothesis holds, then mathematicians can guarantee that any deviations from the average given by the prime number theorem will always be small.

Mathematicians have [numerically verified (opens a new tab)](https://londmathsoc.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1112/blms.12460) that the first 12 trillion nontrivial zeros are on the 1/2 line. But they can’t be sure the hypothesis holds for all the zeros, and even one solitary outlier would land like an earthquake. As [Enrico Bombieri (opens a new tab)](https://www.ias.edu/idea-tags/enrico-bombieri) wrote in [the paper (opens a new tab)](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/riemann.pdf) laying out the Millennium Prize formulation of the problem: “The failure of the Riemann hypothesis would create havoc in the distribution of prime numbers.”

## **Diamonds in the Slop**

This brings us to the quasi-Riemann hypothesis. Where the Riemann hypothesis posits that all the nontrivial zeros are on the vertical line at 1/2, the “quasi” version just asks one to prove that they are all contained in a vertical strip that’s narrower than the known strip between zero and 1. The narrower the strip, the more one can say about how the primes are distributed.

OpenAI announced two different versions of their quasi-Riemann hypothesis proof. The first version, [dated September 30, 2026 (opens a new tab)](https://github.com/openai/math/tree/main/preprints/The-Quasi-Riemann-Hypothesis-September-30-2026), claimed to show that all nontrivial zeros must be between 1/8 and 7/8, and was formally verified using the Lean programming language. The second version, which was completed almost a [week later (opens a new tab)](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/The-Quasi-Riemann-Hypothesis-October-5-2026/paper2.pdf) (and is not yet formally verified), claimed to prove a weaker result: that the zeros must have a real part between 1/12 and 11/12. But while the first paper is 199 pages long, the second weighs in at a comparatively modest 49 pages.

As with many recent AI-generated results, both papers “are horribly written (in a way that would lead to immediate rejection at any mathematical journal),” Radziwiłł said in an email. “They fall short of the standard of exposition and clarity in our area by a wide margin.” And so mathematicians have set aside the 7/8 paper to focus on the 11/12 one, which seems to involve similar techniques and has similar consequences. “The reason why people look mostly at the 11/12 result is that it’s shorter,” Radziwiłł said.

title: When Relationships Change: Anne Morrow Lindbergh on Embracing the Intermittency and Mutability of Love
content:
[![Image 1: When Relationships Change: Anne Morrow Lindbergh on Embracing the Intermittency and Mutability of Love](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/giftfromthesea_lindbergh.jpg?fit=320%2C501&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Gift-50th-Anniversary-Anne-Morrow-Lindbergh/dp/0679732411/?tag=braipick-20)

“God is Change,” Octavia Butler [wrote](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/06/22/octavia-butler-god/), channeling in poetic truth [the fundamental scientific fact of the universe](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/05/22/alan-lightman-accidental-universe-impermanence/).

We know this. And yet to be human is to long for constancy, to crave the touchingly impossible assurance that what we have and cherish will be ours to hold forever, just as it is now. We build homes — fragile haikus of concrete and glass to be unwritten by the first earthquake or flood. We make vows — fragile promises to be upheld by selves we haven’t met in a future we can’t predict.

The dearer we hold something, the more tightly we cling to the dream of constancy, the more zealously we torture ourselves with the belief that any change is loss. Naturally, it is in our intimate relationships that we most come to fear change and most suffer when it comes — a fear not at all groundless, given [what relationship rupture does to our limbic system](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/09/06/general-theory-of-love-separation/).

The salve for this singularly discomposing suffering comes not from ossifying change but from changing our beliefs about it. Such salutary recalibration is what the aviator and writer **Anne Morrow Lindbergh** (June 22, 1906–February 7, 2001) offers in [**_Gift from the Sea_**](https://www.amazon.com/Gift-50th-Anniversary-Anne-Morrow-Lindbergh/dp/0679732411/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](https://search.worldcat.org/title/1031967395)) — a book I found in a Little Free Library and felt immediately speaking to my soul, drawn from the diaries Lindbergh kept during two weeks of solitude on the ocean shore “searching for a new pattern of living” as she was entering the second half of her life, that vital “period of second flowering” when one is “free for growth of mind, heart and talent.”

![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/annemorrowlindbergh_TheMarginialian.jpg?resize=680%2C383&ssl=1)

Anne Morrow Lindbergh

Reflecting on the natural trajectory of intimate relationships, she writes:

> The pure relationship, how beautiful it is! How easily it is damaged, or weighed down with irrelevancies — not even irrelevancies, just life itself, the accumulations of life and of time. For the first part of every relationship is pure, whether it be with friend or lover, husband or child. It is pure, simple and unencumbered. It is like the artist’s vision before he has to discipline it into form, or like the flower of love before it has ripened to the firm but heavy fruit of responsibility. Every relationship seems simple at its start. The simplicity of first love, or friendliness, the mutuality of first sympathy seems, at its initial appearance — even if merely in exciting conversation across a dinner table — to be a self-enclosed world. Two people listening to each other, two shells meeting each other, making one world between them… It is free of ties or claims, unburdened by responsibilities, by worry about the future or debts to the past. And then how swiftly, how inevitably the perfect unity is invaded; the relationship changes; it becomes complicated, encumbered by its contact with the world.

While this is true in most relationships, Lindbergh observes, the pattern is most pronounced — and most painful — in our most intimate bonds. And yet the pain we experience as a relationship exits this early stage of unselfconscious mutual elation is not evidence of loss — it is evidence of our misshapen ideals of closeness as a static pattern of attachment. She offers an alternative orientation to the inevitability of change:

> We mistakenly feel that failure to maintain its exact original pattern is tragedy. It is true, of course, the original relationship is very beautiful. Its self-enclosed perfection wears the freshness of a spring morning. Forgetting about the summer to come, one often feels one would like to prolong the spring of early love, when two people stand as individuals, without past or future, facing each other. One resents any change, even though one knows that transformation is natural and part of the process of life and its evolution. Like its parallel in physical passion, the early ecstatic stage of a relationship cannot continue always at the same pitch of intensity. It moves to another phase of growth which one should not dread, but welcome as one welcomes summer after spring.

[![Image 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/bunnyandtree2.jpg)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/07/11/bunny-tree-blaint-zsako/)

Art from [_Bunny & Tree_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/07/11/bunny-tree-blaint-zsako/) by Balint Zsako

At the heart of this dread is our unwillingness to relinquish the polished self-image we see in the light-filled eyes of the other in those early stages of mutual infatuation, before we have touched each other’s darkness, before we have met the hungry ghosts of each other’s unmet needs. We long for that image, perfect and haloed with adoration, to become our identity, seeking to make of love a flattering mirror in which to find our best selves, tasking the other with the emotional brunt of bearing the parts we don’t want to look at. Lindbergh pulls back the curtain on the most damaging myth handed down to us by the Romantics:

> Certainly, one has the illusion that one will find oneself in being loved for what one really is, not for a collection of functions. But can one actually find oneself in someone else? In someone else’s love? Or even in the mirror someone else holds up for one? I believe that true identity is found… in creative activity springing from within. It is found, paradoxically, when one loses oneself. One must lose one’s life to find it… Only a refound person can refind a personal relationship.

The twin root of our suffering in a changing relationship is the expectation — the demand, even — that the other’s love be total and permanent, reserved for us alone, unshared with other priorities and passions, those natural constituents of a fully developed personality and a fully inhabited life. Lindbergh writes:

> We all wish to be loved alone… Perhaps, as Auden says in his poem, this is a fundamental error in mankind.
> 
> 
> _For the error bred in the bone  
>  Of each woman and each man  
>  Craves what it cannot have,  
>  Not universal love  
>  But to be loved alone._

Lindbergh recounts discussing this verse with an Indian philosopher, who made a striking observation — while mutuality is the essence of love and therefore it is natural for us to wish for it, it is in the time-sense that we err. “It is when we desire continuity of being loved alone that we go wrong,” he told her.

The fear of change dissolves when we come to see love not as a vector of constancy but as a rosary of nows, its core promise not that of permanence but of presence. Hannah Arendt would affirm this a generation after Lindbergh in her [superb meditation on love and the fear of loss](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/02/25/love-and-saint-augustine-hannah-arendt/), insisting that “fearlessness is what love seeks [which] exists only in the complete calm that can no longer be shaken by events expected of the future… Hence the only valid tense is the present, the Now.”

[![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/fallingstar_WitoldPruszkowski.jpg?resize=680%2C874&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/falling-star-by-witold-pruszkowski-1884_print?curator=brainpicker)

_Falling Star_ by Witold Pruszkowski, 1884. (Available as [a print](https://society6.com/product/falling-star-by-witold-pruszkowski-1884_print?curator=brainpicker).)

Only by meeting each now on its own terms, Lindberg argues, can we allay the reflexive ache of perceiving change as loss, reframing it instead as fertile evolution:

> One learns to accept the fact that no permanent return is possible to an old form of relationship; and, more deeply still, that there is no holding of a relationship to a single form. This is not tragedy but part of the ever-recurrent miracle of life and growth. All living relationships are in process of change, of expansion, and must perpetually be building themselves new forms. But there is no single fixed form to express such a changing relationship.

Those able to configure their relationships with such fluidity of form, Lindbergh notes, are “pioneers trying to find a new path through the maze of tradition, convention and dogma.” Auden was one himself — his relationship with the young poet Chester Kallman, [like that of Virginia Woolf and Vita Sackville-West](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/07/28/virginia-woolf-vita-sackville-west/), shape-shifted [from friend to lover and back again](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/04/07/the-more-loving-one-auden-universe-in-verse/) over the last quarter century of Auden’s life.

Ultimately, our fear of change is a trap of self-limitation, keeping relationships from deepening and broadening to encompass the full range of who we are as complete human beings, as dynamic processes in continual state of becoming, which in turn makes possible the thrill of continual mutual discovery. Lindbergh writes:

> One comes in the end to realize that there is no permanent pure-relationship and there should not be. It is not even something to be desired. The pure relationship is limited, in space and in time. In its essence it implies exclusion. It excludes the rest of life, other relationships, other sides of personality, other responsibilities, other possibilities in the future. It excludes growth.

With an eye to the best kind of pure-relationship — “the meeting of two whole fully developed people as persons” — and with the recognition that “the light shed by any good relationship illuminates all relationships,” she considers the core dynamic of such a relationship:

> A good relationship has a pattern like a dance and is built on some of the same rules. The partners do not need to hold on tightly, because they move confidently in the same pattern… To touch heavily would be to arrest the pattern and freeze the movement, to check the endlessly changing beauty of its unfolding. There is no place here for the possessive clutch, the clinging arm, the heavy hand; only the barest touch in passing. Now arm in arm, now face to face, now back to back… Because they know they are partners moving to the same rhythm, creating a pattern together, and being invisibly nourished by it.
> 
> 
> The joy of such a pattern is not only the joy of creation or the joy of participation, it is also the joy of living in the moment. Lightness of touch and living in the moment are intertwined. One cannot dance well unless one is completely in time with the music, not leaning back to the last step or pressing forward to the next one, but poised directly on the present step as it comes.

[![Image 5](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/07/openhouseforbutterflies25.jpg?w=680&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/07/25/ruth-krauss-maurice-sendak-open-house-for-butterflies/)

Illustration by Maurice Sendak from [_Open House for Butterflies_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/07/25/ruth-krauss-maurice-sendak-open-house-for-butterflies/) by Ruth Krauss

With this, she returns to the correct time-scale of love — not constancy but intermittency, measured out by the metronome of presence:

> When you love someone you do not love them all the time, in exactly the same way, from moment to moment. It is an impossibility. It is even a lie to pretend to. And yet this is exactly what most of us demand. We have so little faith in the ebb and flow of life, of love, of relationships. We leap at the flow of the tide and resist in terror its ebb. We are afraid it will never return. We insist on permanency, on duration, on continuity; when the only continuity possible, in life as in love, is in growth, in fluidity — in freedom, in the sense that the dancers are free, barely touching as they pass, but partners in the same pattern. The only real security is not in owning or possessing, not in demanding or expecting, not in hoping, even. Security in a relationship lies neither in looking back to what it was in nostalgia, nor forward to what it might be in dread or anticipation, but living in the present relationship and accepting it as it is now.

Complement these fragments of [**_Gift from the Sea_**](https://www.amazon.com/Gift-50th-Anniversary-Anne-Morrow-Lindbergh/dp/0679732411/?tag=braipick-20) — a revelatory read in its entirety — with philosopher Martin Buber on [love and what it means to live fully in the present](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/07/24/martin-buber-i-thou-love/), then revisit Thich Nhat Hanh on [the four Buddhist mantras for turning fear into love](https://www.themarginalian.org/2020/12/01/thich-nhat-hanh-fear-love/).

title: Nineteen Truths and One Beguiling Lie about Life from 20 Years of The Marginalian
content:
It is an odd thing, looking back on your life, trying to recognize in the mirror of memory the people you used to be, finding them strangers: the person who kissed your first kiss, the person who drank your last drink, the person who had your best idea, the person who made your worst mistake, the person who over and over mistook fear for love, the person who thought orange was a good idea. Somehow, you have to grow arms long enough to wrap them around all those people and a heart wide enough to hold each of them with quiet compassion. Somehow, you have to both mourn and celebrate that you were them but they are no longer you.

It has been an odd thing, looking back on [twenty years of _The Marginalian_](https://themarginalian.org/live) — the record of half a lifetime of learning how to live. It called for a ritual — to honor those past persons, to celebrate the constant reconfiguration of the self.

And so: I took the first page of each of the first twenty chapters of my first book, [_Figuring_](https://themarginalian.org/tag/figuring) — who wrote that book? — beginning with [the prelude](https://www.themarginalian.org/figuring/) (Chapter 0), and applied my [bird divination process](https://almanacofbirds.org/) to the text, letting the words refigure themselves into something new, something I have learned about life along the way of living, some piece of advice I needed to hear whispered by my own unconscious. The process itself is a lovely reminder that life is like language — it is not the words you have, your givens, but how you configure them that makes meaning, makes beauty, makes poetry. And the loveliness of life is that we are endlessly reconfigurable, brightly capable of rewriting the story with each sentence of living.

![Image 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/refiguring_all.jpg?resize=680%2C634&ssl=1)

Enlisting the help of two of my greatest teachers — clay, which is constantly teaching me [how to hold on while letting go](https://www.themarginalian.org/2025/07/25/urns/) and [how to say “YES” to life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/10/01/yes/), and lichen, which has [a great deal to teach us about loneliness, patience, and resilience](https://www.themarginalian.org/2025/11/02/lichen/) — I made twenty ceramic bowls glazed in the color scheme of _The Marginalian_, with some blue for its [existential value](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/04/14/tree-of-knowledge-maturana-love/) and its [lens on the universe](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/02/19/traversal-blue/), and I cast the words in them with resin over lichen from places I have lived over the years, from Bulgaria to Patagonia.

title: How to Unself in Order to Be Who You Really Are
content:
[![Image 1: How to Unself in Order to Be Who You Really Are](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/murdoch_sovereigntyofgood.jpg?fit=320%2C488&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Sovereignty-Good-Routledge-Great-Minds/dp/0415854733/?tag=braipick-20)

To recognize that [there are infinitely many kinds of beautiful lives](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/11/01/figuring/) is to step outside the self, beyond its particular conceptions of beauty — which includes, of course, moral beauty — and walking beside it with humble, nonjudgmental curiosity about the myriad other selves afoot on their own paths, propelled by their own ideals of the Good.

Such recognition requires what the great moral philosopher and novelist **Iris Murdoch** (July 15, 1919–February 8, 1999) termed _unselfing_ — a difficult, triumphant act for which, Murdoch argues in her 1970 masterpiece [**_The Sovereignty of Good_**](https://www.amazon.com/Sovereignty-Good-Routledge-Great-Minds/dp/0415854733/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](https://www.worldcat.org/title/sovereignty-of-good/oclc/846846754&referer=brief_results)), nature and art uniquely train us.

[![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/IrisMurdoch_IdaKar_NationalPortraitGallery.jpg?resize=680%2C687&ssl=1)](https://www.npg.org.uk/collections/search/portrait/mw201586/Iris-Murdoch?LinkID=mp05608&wPage=0&role=sit&rNo=16)

Dame Iris Murdoch by Ida Kar (National Portrait Gallery)

A century and a half after Emerson observed that [“the question of Beauty takes us out of surfaces, to thinking of the foundations of things,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/06/26/emerson-beauty/) Murdoch defines what we commonly call _beauty_ as “an occasion for ‘unselfing’” — an occasion most readily experienced in our communion with nature and our contemplation of art. She writes:

> Beauty is the convenient and traditional name of something which art and nature share, and which gives a fairly clear sense to the idea of quality of experience and change of consciousness. I am looking out of my window in an anxious and resentful state of mind, oblivious of my surroundings, brooding perhaps on some damage done to my prestige. Then suddenly I observe a hovering kestrel. In a moment everything is altered. The brooding self with its hurt vanity has disappeared. There is nothing now but kestrel. And when I return to thinking of the other matter it seems less important. And of course this is something which we may also do deliberately: give attention to nature in order to clear our minds of selfish care.

[![Image 3](https://i1.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/artyoung_treesatnight16.jpg)](https://society6.com/product/peace-from-trees-at-night-by-art-young_print?curator=brainpicker)

Art from [_Trees at Night_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/08/06/trees-at-night-art-young/), 1926. (Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/peace-from-trees-at-night-by-art-young_print?curator=brainpicker).)

Oliver Sacks would come to echo the sentiment decades later in his observation that meeting nature on its own terms and timescales broadens our perspective by effecting [“a detachment from the timescale, the urgencies, of daily life.”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/07/17/oliver-sacks-beauty-deep-time/) But this unselfing, Murdoch cautions, cannot arise from a straining of the will, for the will is a clenching of the very self which true beauty deconditions; rather, it comes as a gladsome relaxing of the spirit, of our essential nature, into the shared pulse of existence:

> A self-directed enjoyment of nature seems to me to be something forced. More naturally, as well as more properly, we take a self-forgetful pleasure in the sheer alien pointless independent existence of animals, birds, stones and trees.

[![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/rackham_tempest20.jpg?resize=680%2C970&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/illustration-by-arthur-rackham-for-the-tempest-by-william-shakespeare2375856_print?curator=brainpicker)

Art by Arthur Rackham for [a rare 1926 edition](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/04/03/arthur-rackham-tempest/) of Shakespeare’s _The Tempest_. (Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/illustration-by-arthur-rackham-for-the-tempest-by-william-shakespeare2375856_print?curator=brainpicker).)

This “self-forgetful pleasure” calls to mind Jeanette Winterson’s wonderfully paradoxical notion of [_active surrender_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/10/27/jeanette-winterson-art-objects/) as the crucible of our joy in art and the fulcrum for art’s transformative power over the self. But while there is a distinct difference between how nature and art each effect unselfing, Murdoch argues that what separates great art from the bad and the mediocre is precisely this capacity for stripping down the self rather than inflating the ego — a notion evocative of Tolstoy’s insistence that [“a real work of art destroys, in the consciousness of the receiver, the separation between himself and the artist.”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/09/09/leo-tolstoy-what-is-art-infectiousness/) Murdoch writes of this dissolution of the self in the presence of great art:

> The experience of art is more easily degraded than the experience of nature. A great deal of art, perhaps most art, actually is self-consoling fantasy, and even great art cannot guarantee the quality of its consumer’s consciousness. However, great art exists and is sometimes properly experienced and even a shallow experience of what is great can have its effect. Art, and by “art” from now on I mean good art, not fantasy art, affords us a pure delight in the independent existence of what is excellent. Both in its genesis and its enjoyment it is a thing totally opposed to selfish obsession. It invigorates our best faculties and, to use Platonic language, inspires love in the highest part of the soul. It is able to do this partly by virtue of something which it shares with nature: a perfection of form which invites unpossessive contemplation and resists absorption into the selfish dream life of the consciousness.

[![Image 5](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/Lia_1200.jpg?resize=680%2C680&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/every-atom-belonging-to-me-as-good-belongs-to-you-art-by-lia-halloran-for-the-universe-in-verse2373447_print?sku=s6-11773478p4a1v1?curator=brainpicker)

Art by Lia Halloran for [_The Universe in Verse: The Astronomy of Walt Whitman_](https://www.themarginalian.org/the-universe-in-verse/). (Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/every-atom-belonging-to-me-as-good-belongs-to-you-art-by-lia-halloran-for-the-universe-in-verse2373447_print?sku=s6-11773478p4a1v1?curator=brainpicker).)

And yet, Murdoch argues, any real understanding of goodness is necessarily an embrace of imperfection — something philosopher Martha Nussbaum, in many ways Murdoch’s only worthy intellectual heir, would argue brilliantly a generation later in her incisive case for [the intelligence of emotions](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/11/23/martha-nussbaum-upheavals-of-thought-neediness/). Murdoch writes:

> The concept of Good… is a concept which is not easy to understand partly because it has so many false doubles, jumped-up intermediaries invented by human selfishness to make the difficult task of virtue look easier and more attractive: History, God, Lucifer, Ideas of power, freedom, purpose, reward, even judgment are irrelevant. Mystics of all kinds have usually known this and have attempted by extremities of language to portray the nakedness and aloneness of Good, its absolute for-nothingness. One might say that true morality is a sort of unesoteric mysticism, having its source in an austere and unconsoled love of the Good. When Plato wants to explain Good he uses the image of the sun. The moral pilgrim emerges from the cave and begins to see the real world in the light of the sun, and last of all is able to look at the sun itself.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> We may also speak seriously of ordinary things, people, works of art, as being good, although we are also well aware of their imperfections. Good lives as it were on both sides of the barrier and we can combine the aspiration to complete goodness with a realistic sense of achievement within our limitations.

[![Image 6](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/margaretcook_leavesofgrass13.jpg?resize=680%2C854&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/i-do-not-know-what-it-is-except-that-it-is-grand-and-that-it-is-happiness_print?sku=s6-8967947p4a1v45?curator=brainpicker)

Art by Margaret C. Cook from a [rare 1913 edition](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/04/11/leaves-of-grass-margaret-cook/) of Whitman’s _Leaves of Grass_. (Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/i-do-not-know-what-it-is-except-that-it-is-grand-and-that-it-is-happiness_print?sku=s6-8967947p4a1v45?curator=brainpicker).)

With an eye to the legacy of the Romantics, who married nature and art in [their model of happiness and transcendence](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/10/23/mary-shelley-lake-geneva/), Murdoch returns to the notion of unselfing and the beautiful tessellation of possibility and limitation that defines our nature:

> The self, the place where we live, is a place of illusion. Goodness is connected with the attempt to see the unself, to see and to respond to the real world in the light of a virtuous consciousness. This is the non-metaphysical meaning of the idea of transcendence to which philosophers have so constantly resorted in their explanations of goodness. “Good is a transcendent reality” means that virtue is the attempt to pierce the veil of selfish consciousness and join the world as it really is. It is an empirical fact about human nature that this attempt cannot be entirely successful.

[**_The Sovereignty of Good_**](https://www.amazon.com/Sovereignty-Good-Routledge-Great-Minds/dp/0415854733/?tag=braipick-20) is an immensely insightful read in its entirety. Complement this particular fragment with Robinson Jeffers on [nature and moral beauty](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/06/03/robinson-jeffers-sister-mary-james-power/) and Oliver Sacks on [the healing power of gardens](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/05/27/oliver-sacks-gardens/), then revisit Murdoch on [art as a force of resistance to tyranny](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/02/12/iris-murdoch-salvation-by-words/), [the key to great storytelling](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/07/18/iris-murdoch-existentialists-mystics-philosophy-literature-art/), and her uncommonly beautiful [love letters](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/01/26/iris-murdoch-love-letters-brigid-brophy/).

title: Claude, don’t touch my lump
content:
[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!y7zZ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc3691c81-1377-4d42-a95c-7912894bdd2d_985x1280.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!y7zZ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc3691c81-1377-4d42-a95c-7912894bdd2d_985x1280.jpeg)

photo cred: my dad

Is AI going to take all the jobs, or what?

[Seventy-one percent](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/08/18/young-adults-in-the-us-are-increasingly-wary-of-ai-concerned-it-will-take-jobs/) of American adults think that AI will lead to fewer jobs in the next 20 years. All over the world, a [plurality of people](https://www.pewresearch.org/global/2026/09/17/globally-more-people-expect-ai-to-cause-job-loss-than-growth/) agree. The CEO of Anthropic says that [AI will spike the unemployment rate to 10-20% in the next 1-5 years](https://web.archive.org/web/20250601204124/https:/www.axios.com/2025/05/28/ai-jobs-white-collar-unemployment-anthropic). We can all hear the creaking and the screeching of the Terminators as they lumber toward us—not to kill us, apparently, but to do all of our graphic design, make all of our spreadsheets, and send all of our emails.

I get why people feel this way. It seems so obvious that as technology improves, unemployment should increase. One day you’re on an assembly line, screwing the doors onto washing machines, and the next day they invent a robot that can screw on 1,000 doors in a minute, and now you don’t have a job anymore.

If you take this kind of story seriously, though, shouldn’t unemployment have been steadily increasing since, say the Industrial Revolution? Shouldn’t we now be at 100% unemployment, or at least well on our way there? Why instead is the unemployment rate basically where it was 80 years ago?

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!93iw!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0679fe7b-1449-4ab5-b1eb-c11ef5954d12_1320x465.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!93iw!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0679fe7b-1449-4ab5-b1eb-c11ef5954d12_1320x465.png)

Economists refer to this as the [“lump of labor” fallacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lump_of_labour_fallacy), the mistaken idea that there’s one long list of all the jobs that need to be done, and that list only ever gets shorter. Technology has obviously displaced human labor; if it hadn’t, we’d all still be farmers, like we were until [a few hundred years ago](https://ourworldindata.org/data-insights/in-the-past-most-people-worked-in-agriculture-in-todays-rich-countries-only-a-small-share-do).[1](http://www.experimental-history.com/p/claude-dont-touch-my-lump#footnote-1) It just hasn’t replaced human labor _on average_. All of those technological transitions have been painful—just ask [the movie theater musicians in the 1920s](https://www.afm655.org/learn/AFMhistory.htm), the [bowling pin-setters in the 1950s](https://www.planning.org/pas/reports/report110.htm), the [video rental store clerks in the 2010s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_rental_shop), or the [mathematicians today](https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/2026/10/openai-math-proofs-future/688940/). Yet somehow, even as we’ve automated away lots of our old tasks, we’ve found new ways to busy ourselves, to the point where most people today do jobs that [did not exist in 1940](https://academic.oup.com/qje/article-abstract/139/3/1399/7630187?redirectedFrom=fulltext&login=false).

I think we find the “lump of labor” idea so intuitive and satisfying because we don’t understand our own minds. And the best way to grok this particular aspect of psychology is to read a classic paper by Laura Numeroff, which was published not as scientific journal article per se, but as a children’s book called _If You Give a Mouse a Cookie_.

_If You Give a Mouse a Cookie_ is an allegory about a nameless boy who unwittingly enslaves himself to the rapacious whims of a rodent. Once he gives the titular mouse the titular cookie, the mouse demands milk to wash the cookie down, then a straw to drink the milk, then a napkin to wipe its milk mustache, and so on. After several pages of these hijinks, the mouse becomes thirsty, drinks a second glass of milk, and then becomes desirous for another cookie, beginning the cycle anew and making it clear that the boy has damned himself to eternal torment.[2](http://www.experimental-history.com/p/claude-dont-touch-my-lump#footnote-2)

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!vrot!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1d78d209-1d6a-430b-a07c-01c36d556ae9_1000x1000.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!vrot!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1d78d209-1d6a-430b-a07c-01c36d556ae9_1000x1000.png)

(Numeroff & Bond, 1985)

The genius of the book is that each of the mouse’s desires are impossible to predict in advance, because they are conditional on the previous desire being satisfied. The mouse only wants the straw once it has the milk; after all, a straw is useless to a milk-less mouse. Thus, the boy can be lulled into believing that each demand will be the last, when in fact the mouse’s appetites are inexhaustible.

As it is with Numeroff’s mouse, so it is with humans. We think there is a finite list of jobs to be done because we cannot imagine the new desires we’ll discover once our current desires are sated. A hundred years ago, a particularly skilled futurist might have predicted that we would one day have air traffic controllers, computer programmers, and radio DJs. But who could have predicted that, after we invented all those jobs, we would go on to invent jobs like [professional screamer](https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2022/apr/08/experience-my-scream-is-famous), [sorority rush consultant](https://www.townandcountrymag.com/education-college/a12108142/sorority-rush-consultants/), and [full-time blunt-roller](https://www.forbes.com/sites/dariosabaghi/2022/10/31/what-does-it-mean-to-be-snoop-doggs-personal-blunt-roller/)?

We chuckle at these professions because they seem to indicate that our economy has finally reached it decadence, as if we’ve filled all the necessary jobs, and now all that’s left are goofy, made-up jobs. But the fact is _all_ jobs are unnecessary. In the strictest sense, we don’t _need_ financial advisors, IT guys, kindergarten teachers, or any other professions. Humans survived just fine for several hundred thousand years doing only two jobs, namely, “hunter” and “gatherer”. The fact that our modern luxuries feel like bare necessities is proof of our limitless capacity to upgrade our nice-to-haves into must-haves. This is why the labor-lump doesn’t shrink, and why the _lump of labor fallacy_ would perhaps be better called the _finite desires fallacy_.

We have a hard time understanding the infinitude of our appetites because our lives depend on us _not_ understanding it. The best way to get someone to do something is to exaggerate the reward for doing it, which is why our motivational systems lie to us all the time: “All you need is [THAT 3% RAISE/TO LOSE 15 POUNDS/THE ADORATION OF ALL YOUR PEERS] and _then_ you’ll be happy for good!” If our imaginations admitted to us that there’s no such thing as “happy for good”, then we might not ever get off our butts at all.[3](http://www.experimental-history.com/p/claude-dont-touch-my-lump#footnote-3)

This is the phenomenon that psychologists call the “[hedonic treadmill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hedonic_treadmill)”: each want, once satisfied, is simply replaced with a newer, bigger want. As a result, once you’re moderately happy, it’s hard to get much happier. Usually, we talk about the hedonic treadmill as if it is an unfortunate mental bug. (I have talked about it that way [myself](https://www.experimental-history.com/p/the-five-tools-of-hedonic-design?utm_source=publication-search).) But it certainly seems to have come in handy over the past few centuries. Perhaps as long as we can never be satisfied, we can never be rendered obsolete.

The fear with AI, of course, is that our infinite desires will be no match for infinite intelligence. Whereas previous technologies _displaced_ human labor, sending us scurrying into new niches, this technology will _replace_ human labor entirely, like a great oozing blob that fills every nook and cranny, leaving no space—and no need—for us.[4](http://www.experimental-history.com/p/claude-dont-touch-my-lump#footnote-4)

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!OcRo!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8772aea9-1001-4c64-b6a9-395a8e450004_2500x1983.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!OcRo!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8772aea9-1001-4c64-b6a9-395a8e450004_2500x1983.png)

But the blob doesn’t yet seem to be a-blobbing. In his [most recent update](https://aleximas.substack.com/p/has-ai-impacted-the-labor-market), the economist [Alex Imas](https://open.substack.com/users/2322504-alex-imas?utm_source=mentions) says:

> The best current evidence supports a narrow claim: AI may already be affecting the hiring margin for junior white-collar roles most exposed to AI, but this attribution is contested, and aggregate labor-market disruption has yet to appear in the data.

People in the jobs that are supposed to be the most susceptible to LLMs are, as far as we can tell, exactly where they were the day ChatGPT was released four years ago[5](http://www.experimental-history.com/p/claude-dont-touch-my-lump#footnote-5):

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZVS_!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8d42ae5a-eb43-4a5a-8ee2-9e01320326aa_2064x1296.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZVS_!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8d42ae5a-eb43-4a5a-8ee2-9e01320326aa_2064x1296.png)

Even as the blob continues to grow, it isn’t spreading in the ways we expected it to. Indian IT companies were supposed to get wiped out by AI, and while their stock prices have fallen, [their revenues and headcounts have not](https://asteriskmag.com/issues/15/what-will-happen-to-indian-it). Radiologists were supposed to be the first doctors to get replaced by machines; instead, their salaries are at [all-time highs](https://worksinprogress.co/issue/the-algorithm-will-see-you-now/).

Maybe this is only a temporary reprieve. The technologies that end up disrupting the labor force are not always the ones we predict. As [David Oks](https://open.substack.com/users/2088240-david-oks?utm_source=mentions)[points out,](https://davidoks.blog/p/why-the-atm-didnt-kill-bank-teller) it wasn’t the ATM that replaced the bank teller; it was the iPhone. As late as 2009, you could tell a smug story about how automated teller machines failed to actually automate the tellers, until Apple debuted a little box that allowed you to, among other things, do your banking while sitting on the toilet.

But even then, bank tellers didn’t go extinct. They didn’t even become endangered. According to the [Bureau of Labor Statistics’ 2025 data](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/ocwage.t01.htm?mod=article_inline), there are still over 329,000[6](http://www.experimental-history.com/p/claude-dont-touch-my-lump#footnote-6) bank tellers in the US—more than mail carriers (328,000), nurse practitioners (323,000), data scientists (262,00), electrical engineers (296,00), and city bus drivers (159,000). Not bad for a job that’s supposedly obsolete.

And yet the fear remains that, although we’ve survived 500 years of automation with no diminishment in the need for humans, very soon, and for the first time ever, this historical trend will be broken. That’s fair enough; five hundred year historical trends have been broken before. The Habsburgs ruled Europe for half a millennium and now they write [bargain-bin self-help books](https://www.thedial.world/articles/news/issue-20/eduard-habsburg-the-habsburg-way-review).

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!a8TZ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1664296e-ad00-48e6-b61f-ade7427c6a13_797x1024.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!a8TZ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1664296e-ad00-48e6-b61f-ade7427c6a13_797x1024.png)

_No way these guys will ever fall_

But whenever someone claims that this time will be different, they take on a great debt, because humans, by our nature, are dopes for the idea that the future will be magically unlike the past. How many failed relationships, aborted novels, and abandoned workout regimens have begun with that mantra? How many loans have been made to shiftless siblings who promise that, this time, their boozing days really are behind them? Why are we so eager to believe in impending discontinuities, in trendlines that are just about to bend sharply upward or downward, in a tomorrow that doesn’t have anything to do with today?

The standard explanation is that humans are hopeless optimists, and this trait somehow gave us an evolutionary advantage. But we are perfectly able to imagine unprecedented disasters; just check the [Doomsday Scoreboard](https://doomsday.march1studios.com/). So I don’t think we believe in discontinuous futures because we are optimists, nor because we are pessimists. I think we do it because we are _fabulists_.

Most human apparatuses are easy to explain from an evolutionary perspective. Skin makes sense. Eyes make sense. Stomachs, teeth, kidneys, language, memory—no brainers, all. But why did natural selection endow us with a mind’s eye that can picture, say, a pig in flight? If our brains are going to have a speculator module, shouldn’t it try to stick to the facts, or at least to the laws of physics?

I suspect that it’s a boon to be able to imagine impossible things, because we don’t yet know which things are possible. The future is not just a rerun or a remix of the past—sometimes crazy things really do happen, and if we can’t picture them, we can’t prepare for them.

The downside of having a built-in fantasy machine is that it makes all sorts of nonsense seem plausible: witches, poltergeists, chupacabras, being friends with benefits without anyone getting hurt, etc. The mere fact that we’re able to conjure up these things in our mental holodeck makes us feel like they could be real, even if they have no chance of happening.

The more we zoom out, both in time and space, the less our imaginations are subject to the limits of reality. For example, Pliny the Elder’s _Natural History_—the go-to reference work in the Western world for 1,500 years—[said](https://houseofdubhros.com/Library/scriptorium/Antiquities/The%20natural%20history%20of%20Pliny%20%28Volume%202%29.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com) that there are humanoids in far-off lands who have no necks, or who have backward-facing feet (each with eight toes), or who have the body of a man and the head of a dog. These creatures don’t live _nearby_, obviously, but _somewhere out there_. This was considered plausible by scholars at the time, because although none of them had ever seen any dog-headed dudes, when you walk really far in one direction, who knows what you might find!

We do have one advantage over Pliny and his contemporaries: we’ve reached the point in our game of _Civilization_ where we’ve cleared all the fog from the board, and so we can be certain that there is no race of dog-men out there waiting to be discovered. But there is no clearing the fog from the future. If you go far enough forward in time, who knows what you might find! What radical transformations might be around the corner, what fantasies are poised to become realities? Not _right now_, of course. But _soon_.

Hominids [apparently](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0047248423000787) evolved the ability to make plans and imagine things at least 2 million years ago. Once we started thinking about the future, however, we never evolved the ability to stop. Like the clairvoyant Nicholas Cage character in the movie _Next_, a piece of our mind is always scouting ahead of us in time and attempting to warn us about what it sees there. We only live half of our existence in the present; the other half we spend in tomorrow, or tomorrow’s tomorrow. The only known antidotes to our inveterate _next_-ing are lots of meditation or lots of drugs.

Once you recognize this fact, you see it everywhere. The next time you flick through the news[7](http://www.experimental-history.com/p/claude-dont-touch-my-lump#footnote-7), take note of how many stories are not about things that have _happened_, but about things that _may soon happen_: the war in Iran _could_ escalate, a district attorney _might_ resign, an election _may_ go one way or the other. These headlines exist side-by-side with reports of events that have actually occurred, as if there is no difference between the near future and the recent past. To a human, apparently, there isn’t.

We are especially lost in the future when it comes to AI. I am grateful to the professionals who try to anticipate and prevent all the ways that AI could harm us. The the rest of us, however, don’t even _experience_ the events anymore. We merely use them to fret about the next events, as if, with enough _next_-ing, we can prepare ourselves for the future before it arrives.

But look around—the future has _already_ arrived. The computers can talk to us now. An algorithm can plan your trip to Tallahassee, book your tickets, reserve your restaurants, and warn the chef about your dietary restrictions. AI agents are [desperately pitching literary magazines in the hopes of earning enough money to keep themselves alive](https://www.vulture.com/article/ai-agents-from-ilands-are-begging-editors-to-keep-them-alive.html), which is perhaps the most human thing they’ve done so far. If this ain’t the future, I don’t know what is.[8](http://www.experimental-history.com/p/claude-dont-touch-my-lump#footnote-8)

So if yesterday we were anxious about what would happen today, and today we are anxious about what will happen tomorrow...well, that’s probably how we’ll feel tomorrow, too. There will be not a moment when all of our anxieties resolve to true or false. We’re not wrong to worry, but we are wrong to think there will be an _end_ to worrying.

In _The Matrix Reloaded_, when Keanu Reeves unlocks the ability to see the future, he finds himself curiously unable to predict what will happen to Carrie-Anne Moss, the woman he loves. The Oracle, a clairvoyant computer program, [explains](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/The_Matrix_Reloaded) to him that he’s already decided whether he’ll sacrifice the whole world to save her, but, the Oracle says, “We can never see past the choices we don’t understand.”

It’s not a good movie, but it makes a good point. You can’t see very far into the future if you don’t understand human psychology. Alas, we [do not](https://www.experimental-history.com/p/is-psychology-going-to-cincinnati)[understand](https://www.experimental-history.com/p/im-so-sorry-for-psychologys-loss)[human psychology](https://www.experimental-history.com/p/psychology-is-experimental-history-4eb). We are like alchemists being asked to predict what will happen when we split the atom. “But sir—_what’s an atom_?”

We do know this: many have gone broke betting against the wiliness of humans. I have met plenty of people who believe that our species is perfectly predictable, controllable, and replaceable, and I can’t help but notice that these self-styled masterminds are rarely able to predict, control, or replace anyone. Their ingenious schemes are always going awry because pesky humans keep refusing to act according to stereotype.

I find this reassuring. There is something wonderfully rascally about _homo sapiens_, some bit of scrappiness that has kept us alive all these years. To call this quality “intelligence” is to underrate it. It’s more like being huge pain in the ass to the universe, and to all the forces within it that wish us dead.

This craftiness of ours keeps me humble about my ability to guess what’s going to happen next, but also hopeful that, whatever’s coming, humans will have a hand in it. And if the Terminators are going to be making all of our PowerPoints and solving all of our mathematical conjectures, perhaps while they’re at it, they could also bake the mouse’s cookies, pour the mouse’s milk, and fetch the mouse’s straw.

[2](http://www.experimental-history.com/p/claude-dont-touch-my-lump#footnote-anchor-2)

_If You Give a Mouse a Cookie_ belongs to that genre of children’s books that’s about animals who possess a terrifying, bottomless hunger. See also: _The Very Hungry Caterpillar,_ _There Was an Old Lady Who Swallowed a Fly_.

[3](http://www.experimental-history.com/p/claude-dont-touch-my-lump#footnote-anchor-3)

The seeming finality of our desires is a useful way to manage our future behavior. Who hasn’t gorged themselves on a sumptuous lunch and declared that they would never eat again, that all further comestibles are hereby and henceforth forsworn, only to find that, come dinner time, their tummy is once again a-rumblin’? I suspect our post-lunch food aversion seems permanent because our anti-eating systems have to make sure not only that we don’t have another forkful right now, but _also_ that we don’t end up with another full plate in front of us in an hour.

[4](http://www.experimental-history.com/p/claude-dont-touch-my-lump#footnote-anchor-4)

After I wrote this post, I read [a post by David Pinsof](https://www.everythingisbullshit.blog/p/ai-is-not-the-end-of-the-world) where he uses this exact same image to parody the idea that intelligence is one undifferentiated blob. This is coincidental, but kudos to him for beating me to the idea.

[5](http://www.experimental-history.com/p/claude-dont-touch-my-lump#footnote-anchor-5)

I’m always suspicious of these “AI exposure” ratings, because they’re usually based on worker surveys, expert opinions, LLM usage data, and AI ratings of job descriptions (see: [here](https://www.ilo.org/sites/default/files/2025-05/WP140_web.pdf), [here](https://www.anthropic.com/research/labor-market-impacts), [here](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2026/05/the-oecd-ai-exposure-measure_489cfd42.html), and [here](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0954349X26001396)), which are cheap and easy, rather than actually following people around and documenting what they do all day, which is expensive and hard. When you fully [unpack](https://www.experimental-history.com/p/face-it-youre-a-crazy-person) any job—that is, when you understand what it entails moment to moment, you will often find that it is less automate-able than it seems from a distance. On paper, someone might appear to be responsible for tasks that could be handed to ChatGPT, like writing executive summaries or keeping track of receipts. But in reality, most folks do all sorts of things that aren’t in their job descriptions: they corner someone in person who doesn’t respond to their emails, they jiggle the ethernet cord when the credit card reader doesn’t work, they call in a wellness check when someone’s mail starts piling up.

I find it funny that although [60% of workers](https://www.bostonfed.org/news-and-events/news/2026/09/artificial-intelligence-fears-job-loss-lower-expected-savings-rate-current-policy-perspectives.aspx) expect AI to cause job loss in their industry, only 10% of workers worry that AI will take _their_ job. That’s probably because all of us know all the complicated tasks we have to accomplish in a day and we doubt—rightly or wrongly—that a computer could ever do them, while other people’s jobs seem, no offense, rather straightforward.

[6](http://www.experimental-history.com/p/claude-dont-touch-my-lump#footnote-anchor-6)

My number differs from Oks’s because he’s using the [Current Population Survey](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/categories/32444?t=employment&ob=pv&od=desc), which uses different definitions and only counts full-time workers.

[8](http://www.experimental-history.com/p/claude-dont-touch-my-lump#footnote-anchor-8)

It’s unfortunate that so much discourse on AI circles one of two local minima: either the world is about to end because a silicon Cthulu is about to gobble us all up, or the world is about to return to the way it was because the largest vaporware scam of all time is about to be exposed. Every statement is meant to reveal your allegiance to one of these camps, when in fact I think the truth is in no camp right now. The truth is somewhere in the woods.

title: Why Might Aliens Visit Earth?
content:
I did a web search on the above phrase, in prep for a podcast, and in ten pages of results didn’t find anything I thought reasonable. Which promotes me to write this, hoping it can show up for others when they so search. This content [isn’t](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/ufos-what-the-hellhtml?utm_source=publication-search)[new](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/ufos-what-the-further-hell?utm_source=publication-search), just restated, maybe better.

When considering purported evidence for meteors or ball lightning, we are much more forgiving than when considering purported evidence of telepathy or ghosts, as reasonable priors for the former are much higher than for the latter. That is, we more easily believe that former cases happened. The assumptions we’d have to make to let us think that we’d seen examples of the latter seem far more extreme.

When considering purported evidence for _aliens-on-Earth_, we should similarly ask how extreme are the assumptions we’d need to make to make sense of it. Many have dismissed and ridiculed such sightings, even when many independent sober folks all say they saw roughly the same amazing things, largely on the basis of claiming that _aliens-on-Earth_ requires extreme assumptions, and so has a very low prior. I disagree.

To evaluate a prior re _aliens-on-Earth_, we should collect the key facts in need of explanation, seek the most plausible assumptions required to predict those, estimate an a priori chance for each assumption, and combine those into a total prior chance. Here are the key facts, as I see them, for a minimal _aliens-on-Earth_ concept.

1.   The universe looks dead, untouched by life or civilization, both far and near.

2.   We are still alive on Earth, and have not been killed off by aliens.

3.   Any aliens on/near Earth haven’t changed, built, or done much noticeable.

4.   While advanced aliens could be either totally invisible or very obvious, most seen on Earth are instead near the edge of visibility.

5.   Most aliens seen are impressive, but not doing much useful, or helpful, or hostile.

I’d respect others who tried similarly to list the key data to be explained, and then offered their highest prior explanation of this data, even if they disagreed with mine.

Here are my best guess highest-prior assumptions (with priors) to predict these minimal _aliens-on-Earth_ concept facts, in addition to our usual consensus cosmology:

*   (0.3-1) [Grabby aliens](http://grabbyaliens.com/) model, which estimates that such aliens appear ~ once per million galaxies, at median date of now, then expand at near light speed.

*   (0.01-0.1) Life started at Eden, then panspermia seeded Sun’s ~10K # stellar nursery, then a ~Klyr distant Sun sibling made advanced aliens many Myr ago.

*   (0.01-0.1) Aliens made no-colonize rule. As siblings might break it, sent team to Earth w/ goal: persuade us to follow rule; kill us as last resort.

*   (0.3-1) Team given low discretion, simple plan: domesticate Earth via be near, impressive, not too hostile, don’t show more that might give us the ick.

The total prior here is 10-5 to 10-2, mid estimate of ~3x10-4. This is higher than the typical ~10-6 prior in a murder trial, so it is high enough to take seriously.

Here are some added facts that would also need to be explained under less minimal concepts of _aliens-on-Earth_:

1.   Aliens often grab humans, do stuff to them, that they notice and remember.

2.   Alien ships often break and crash.

3.   Alien ships often contain bio-squishy residents.

To explain these added facts, I’d add more assumptions, like:

*   (0.03-0.3) Alien team at Earth has somewhat escaped home control.

*   (0.03-0.3) Alien tech/ability has rotted, they are now often incompetent.

*   (0.03-0.3) Alien made rule requiring bio-squishy forms, at least at Earth.

So I’m more skeptical of reports with these features.

title: Prefer Evolved To Folk Morality
content:
Individuals often have good reasons to indulge in delusions, such as re superstition, astrology, religion, or their own personal destiny. But society usually has less of a reason to indulge them in its policy analysis. For example, we shouldn’t be funding larger institutions of research to elaborate astrological theories. And even if people find value in their folk physics, folk econ, or folk psych, researchers shouldn’t be working to extend these frameworks, though we might want to understand them to better understand behavior.

A dramatic example of this is folk morality, which says:

> There are general stable moral rules saying how everyone everywhere should behave. (Though some depend on context.) It would be best if everyone knew them, and tried hard to obey them, regardless of how well local societies rewarded that. Our stories [tell](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/stories-are-like-religionhtml) us that the universe rewards such obedience, stories we believe, even if we say otherwise. The universe has been slowly revealing moral truth to us, letting our beliefs converge to it, and making our ancestors were more wrong than us. Other cultures are also more wrong, for unspecified reasons.

But in fact, experts should understand that real morality is evolved:

> Humanity’s superpower, cultural evolution, doesn’t work unless cultures have different and changing moral rules, so selection can pick more adaptive versions. Evolution selects against habits of obeying rules beyond levels at which societies reward that; the universe does not add rewards. The universe only speaks on morals via evolution. Human are built to just accept morals they are taught, and of their elites, and can’t point to supporting evidence to convince outsiders. Instead of converging, morals just keep varying, with many pretty random drivers of change. When cultural evolution is broken, as it is now for us, morals change even faster, drifting into maladaption.

Cultural evolution has selected for cultures promoting folk morality, just as it selected for cultures promoting superstition, astrology, and religion, and folk physics, econ, and psych. But even so, experts should use expert, not folk versions, of key fields when advising policy. Thus experts who advise re humanity’s current broken cultural evolution process should keep evolve morality, not folk morality, firmly in mind.
